books.section: A. The Chesapeake and the Upper South

options.misconception: The table shows exports growing, not failing — the first shipments were the start, not the end.
options.text: Tobacco stopped being grown after the first shipments failed.
Tobacco grew from a first shipment into the region's leading export.

options.misconception: Rice belonged to the lower South, not the Chesapeake — the table is about tobacco's rise, not its replacement.
options.text: Tobacco was replaced by rice as the Chesapeake's main crop.

options.misconception: The 1750 row says the opposite — tobacco was nearly three-fourths of the region's exports.
options.text: Tobacco exports fell to almost nothing by 1750.

rationales.A: The table shows exports growing, not failing — the first shipments were the start, not the end.
rationales.B: The table runs one way: a first shipment in 1617, more than 35 million pounds a year by 1700, and nearly three-fourths of the region's exports by 1750.
rationales.C: Rice belonged to the lower South, not the Chesapeake — the table is about tobacco's rise, not its replacement.
rationales.D: The 1750 row says the opposite — tobacco was nearly three-fourths of the region's exports.
rationales.general:
1. Read the table like a timeline. First shipment, then millions of pounds, then three-fourths of everything the region sold.
2. Ask what the direction means. Tobacco did not stay a small crop — it took over the Chesapeake's economy.
3. Name the pattern. One crop, grown for export, came to define a whole region.
Remember: when a table runs in one direction, follow it — the trend is the argument.

source: original; data table drawn from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 4
stem: According to the table, what happened to tobacco in the Chesapeake between 1617 and 1750?

stimulus.text:
| Year | Tobacco in the Chesapeake |
|---|---|
| 1617 | First shipments sent to England |
| 1700 | More than 35 million pounds exported in a year |
| 1750 | Nearly three-fourths of the Chesapeake's exports, and nearly one-third of all exports from British North America |
